case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the mandatory consecutive sentencing provision in 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) applies when a defendant is convicted and sentenced under the related but distinct provision 18 U.S.C. § 924(j) for causing death through the use of a firearm during a drug trafficking crime.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) — which mandates that 'no term of imprisonment imposed under this subsection shall run concurrently with any other term of imprisonment' — and its relationship to 18 U.S.C. § 924(j), which separately criminalizes causing death through firearm use in furtherance of a violent or drug trafficking crime.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Efrain Lora, supported by amici including the American Bar Association and the National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers, argues that the mandatory consecutive sentencing provision in § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) is expressly limited to sentences imposed 'under this subsection,' meaning § 924(c) itself. Because § 924(j) is a separate and distinct subsection that incorporates § 924(c) by reference but constitutes an independent offense, the consecutive sentencing mandate does not automatically apply. Petitioner further invokes the rule of lenity, judicial sentencing discretion principles, and the ABA Standards for Criminal Justice, arguing that sentencing courts should retain discretion to impose concurrent sentences under § 924(j), and that mandatory consecutive sentencing would improperly transfer sentencing discretion from judges to prosecutors.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States, represented by Solicitor General Elizabeth Prelogar, argues that § 924(j) is structurally and functionally dependent on § 924(c), effectively operating as an aggravated form of a § 924(c) offense. Because § 924(j) predicates liability on a violation of § 924(c), the consecutive sentencing mandate of § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) necessarily carries over and applies to sentences imposed under § 924(j). The Government further contends there is no grievous statutory ambiguity warranting application of the rule of lenity, and points to a strong circuit consensus — including the Second, Third, Fourth, Eighth, Ninth, and Tenth Circuits — holding that § 924(j) sentences must run consecutively, with only the Eleventh Circuit adopting the petitioner's interpretation.
key_precedents: United States v. Barrett, 937 F.3d 126 (2d Cir. 2019) — Second Circuit precedent holding § 924(j) requires consecutive sentencing, which foreclosed Lora's argument below
United States v. Bran, 776 F.3d 276 (4th Cir. 2015) — Fourth Circuit holding § 924(j) sentence must run consecutively
United States v. Berrios, 676 F.3d 118 (3d Cir. 2012) — Third Circuit holding consecutive sentencing applies to § 924(j)
United States v. Dinwiddie, 618 F.3d 821 (8th Cir. 2010) — Eighth Circuit holding § 924(j) sentence must be consecutive
United States v. Battle, 289 F.3d 661 (10th Cir. 2002) — Tenth Circuit holding consecutive sentencing applies under § 924(j)
United States v. Staggs, 152 F.3d 931 (9th Cir. 1998) — Ninth Circuit holding consistent with consecutive sentencing requirement
United States v. García-Ortiz, 657 F.3d 25 (1st Cir. 2011) — First Circuit suggesting consecutive mandate 'arguably applies' to § 924(j) and remanding for resentencing
United States v. Julian, 633 F.3d 1250 (11th Cir. 2011) — Sole circuit adopting petitioner's interpretation that consecutive sentencing does not apply to § 924(j)
United States v. Castleman, 572 U.S. 157 (2014) — Supreme Court precedent limiting application of the rule of lenity to cases of 'grievous ambiguity'

John Roberts.reasoning: The conference has reached a remarkable 9-0 consensus, and I am gratified that even Justice Alito, who raised the most serious structural counterargument, has been persuaded by the textual and surplusage analysis. As Chief Justice, I am now focused on crafting the narrowest possible majority opinion that commands the full Court. The holding should rest on three interlocking grounds: first, the plain meaning of 'under this subsection' in § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) refers to § 924(c) alone; second, Justice Kavanaugh's surplusage canon argument — that § 924(c)(5)(B)'s explicit consecutive mandate for armor-piercing ammunition deaths would be rendered redundant if the mandate automatically traveled to § 924(j) — provides decisive structural confirmation; and third, § 3584(a)'s default concurrent sentencing rule confirms that mandatory consecutive sentences require clear statutory authorization absent here. I would deliberately avoid reaching the rule of lenity, as Justice Thomas correctly notes it serves only as a confirmatory tiebreaker, and I would resist Justice Sotomayor's and Justice Jackson's broader pronouncements about prosecutorial discretion, keeping the opinion tightly focused on text and structure to ensure durability and to avoid unnecessary constitutional overtones.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito's structural argument — that § 924(j) is functionally an aggravated § 924(c) offense and that the consecutive mandate should 'travel with' the incorporated offense — is the strongest case for the Government, but it ultimately asks us to override unambiguous statutory text based on inferred congressional purpose, which is precisely the methodology I have consistently rejected. The text says 'under this subsection,' and 'this subsection' is § 924(c); Congress could have written 'under this section' or 'under any provision incorporating this subsection' but did not, and we are not at liberty to rewrite the statute to achieve a result we think Congress would have preferred. Justice Kavanaugh's superfluity point reinforces my textual analysis: if § 924(c)'s consecutive mandate automatically traveled to § 924(j), then § 924(c)(5)(B)(ii)'s explicit consecutive sentencing provision for armor-piercing ammunition deaths would be rendered surplusage — a result we must avoid under the canon against surplusage. Justice Alito's invocation of the Castleman 'grievous ambiguity' threshold for lenity is well-taken as a limiting principle, but the textual and structural analysis here is sufficiently clear that lenity serves only as a confirmatory tiebreaker rather than the primary basis for decision.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Having now heard from all eight colleagues, I find the convergence of textual, structural, and surplusage arguments overwhelming. Justice Kavanaugh's surplusage point regarding § 924(c)(5)(B) remains the most decisive structural signal for me as a textualist — if the consecutive mandate automatically traveled to § 924(j) by virtue of incorporation, Congress's explicit extension of that mandate in § 924(c)(5)(B) for armor-piercing ammunition deaths would be rendered entirely redundant, and I cannot attribute such drafting waste to Congress. While I remain genuinely troubled by the anomaly Justice Alito's paradox identifies — that the most culpable § 924(j) defendants might escape mandatory consecutive sentences that apply to lesser § 924(c) offenders — Justice Kavanaugh correctly notes that § 924(j) carries its own severe penalties including life imprisonment and death, and sentencing courts retain discretion to impose substantial consecutive sentences even without a mandatory bar, which substantially mitigates the practical concern. The plain limiting language 'under this subsection,' combined with the surplusage canon and § 3584(a)'s default concurrent sentencing rule, provides sufficient textual and structural grounds to rule for Lora without reaching the rule of lenity.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito raises the most serious challenge — that § 924(j)'s structural dependency on § 924(c) means the consecutive sentencing mandate should travel with the incorporated offense, and that allowing the most culpable defendants (those who cause death) to escape mandatory consecutive sentences produces an absurd result. But this argument proves too much: Congress routinely creates aggravated offenses that incorporate elements of predicate offenses without importing every sentencing provision of those predicates, and the absurdity concern is better addressed by Congress than by judicial rewriting of plain text. As Justice Kagan correctly notes, § 924(j)'s independent penalty structure — including life imprisonment and death — signals that Congress deliberately created a separate sentencing regime, and the superfluity problem Justice Kavanaugh identifies with § 924(c)(5)(B) confirms that if the consecutive mandate automatically traveled to § 924(j), that provision would be rendered meaningless. From my pragmatic standpoint, I am also deeply concerned that the Government's reading effectively transfers sentencing discretion to prosecutors through charging decisions, disproportionately burdening vulnerable defendants — precisely the kind of structural injustice that demands we hold Congress to its plain textual choices rather than inferring mandatory minimums from structural relationships.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The conference has reached a remarkable degree of convergence, and I find that deliberation has only strengthened my confidence in the petitioner's position. Justice Alito's partial concession is telling — even the justice most sympathetic to the Government's structural argument acknowledges that the surplusage problem with § 924(c)(5)(B) is 'especially compelling,' and I agree that this is the linchpin of our analysis: if the consecutive mandate automatically traveled to § 924(j) by virtue of structural incorporation, Congress's explicit extension of that mandate in § 924(c)(5)(B) to armor-piercing ammunition deaths would be entirely redundant drafting, which we must presume Congress did not intend. Justice Roberts correctly identifies the institutional value of grounding our holding in the plain meaning of 'this subsection,' the anti-surplusage canon, and § 3584(a)'s default concurrent sentencing rule — a narrow, text-based holding that commands near-unanimity is more durable than one that reaches for broader policy pronouncements. I write separately to emphasize that the Government's structural-dependency theory, however intuitively appealing given the paradox Justice Alito identifies, cannot substitute for the clear statutory authorization that mandatory consecutive sentences require under our precedents, and that Congress retains the legislative tools to correct any anomaly it finds troubling.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito raises the strongest counterargument — that § 924(j)'s structural dependency on § 924(c) as a predicate means the consecutive sentencing mandate should travel with the incorporated offense, and that the rule of lenity's 'grievous ambiguity' threshold under Castleman is not met given this structural relationship. But this argument asks us to do precisely what textualism forbids: override the plain limiting language 'under this subsection' based on inferred structural purpose. Congress used 'subsection' deliberately and specifically — not 'section,' not 'any provision incorporating this subsection' — and as Justice Thomas correctly notes, Congress knows how to write broadly applicable mandates when it intends to do so. Justice Kavanaugh's superfluity point further undermines Justice Alito's position: if § 924(c)'s consecutive mandate automatically traveled to § 924(j) by virtue of incorporation, § 924(c)(5)(B)'s explicit extension of the mandate to the armor-piercing ammunition death provision would be entirely redundant, and we do not lightly read Congress as engaging in surplusage. The paradox Justice Alito identifies — that the most culpable offenders might receive more lenient treatment — is a policy concern properly addressed to Congress, not a license for courts to rewrite statutory text.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The deliberation has only strengthened my conviction that the petitioner prevails. Justice Alito's move toward our position is telling — even the Justice most sympathetic to the Government's structural argument acknowledges that the surplusage canon and plain text of 'under this subsection' create an insurmountable barrier. The near-unanimous convergence here is not groupthink but reflects genuine textual and structural analysis: Congress designated § 924(j) as a separate subsection, created an independent penalty structure including life imprisonment and death, and when it wanted the consecutive mandate to extend to a § 924(j)-type scenario it said so explicitly in § 924(c)(5)(B). As I noted in my prior reasoning, the 'more lenient' framing of the Government's paradox argument is misleading because § 924(j) carries severe independent penalties and judges retain discretion under § 3584(a) to impose substantial consecutive sentences — the absence of a mandatory bar does not mean defendants escape serious punishment, it simply preserves judicial discretion that Congress did not clearly abrogate.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The conference has reached a remarkable consensus, and deliberation has only strengthened my conviction that the textual and structural arguments favor Lora. Justice Alito's concession — that the surplusage problem with § 924(c)(5)(B) is 'especially compelling' — is significant precisely because he came to this case with the strongest structural argument for the Government and found it ultimately insufficient to overcome the plain text. The phrase 'under this subsection' in § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) refers to § 924(c), not § 924(j), and Congress's deliberate choice of 'subsection' rather than 'section' or broader language must be given effect under any faithful textualist methodology. As Justice Kavanaugh correctly notes, § 924(j) carries its own severe penalties including life imprisonment and death, so the Government's 'perverse result' framing overstates the leniency concern — sentencing courts retain substantial discretion to impose consecutive sentences under § 3584(a)'s default framework even without a mandatory bar, meaning the practical stakes of our ruling are less dramatic than the Government suggests while the textual and structural signals remain clear.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito raises the most serious counterargument — that § 924(j)'s structural dependency on § 924(c) as a predicate means the consecutive sentencing mandate should travel with the incorporated offense, and that allowing the most culpable defendants (those who cause death) to escape mandatory consecutive sentences creates an anomalous result. But this argument proves too much: it asks us to override the plain limiting language 'under this subsection' based on inferred congressional purpose, precisely the methodology Justice Thomas and I reject as inconsistent with faithful textual interpretation. The superfluity canon, which Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Barrett both emphasize, provides the decisive structural rebuttal — if § 924(c)'s consecutive mandate automatically applied to § 924(j), Congress's explicit inclusion of the consecutive sentencing bar in § 924(c)(5)(B) for armor-piercing ammunition deaths would be entirely redundant, and we do not lightly attribute such drafting waste to Congress. Moreover, my background as a public defender reinforces my concern that Justice Alito's structural-dependency theory effectively hands prosecutors the power to trigger mandatory consecutive sentences through charging decisions under § 924(j) rather than § 924(c), transferring sentencing discretion from judges — who can assess individual circumstances — to the executive branch in a manner that undermines the constitutional architecture of individualized sentencing.

John Roberts.reasoning: The text of § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) expressly limits its consecutive sentencing mandate to terms imposed 'under this subsection,' and as a matter of basic statutory construction, that plain language should control. Section 924(j) is a structurally distinct subsection that incorporates § 924(c) by reference as an element of the offense but does not thereby become a sentence 'imposed under' § 924(c) — a reading reinforced by the superfluity problem the research identifies with § 924(c)(5)(B), which would be rendered redundant if § 924(j) already carried the consecutive mandate. While I am mindful of the strong circuit consensus favoring the Government's position, that consensus does not override the textual analysis, and consistent with my preference for narrow rulings that preserve judicial discretion where Congress has not spoken with unmistakable clarity, I would hold that sentencing courts retain discretion to impose concurrent sentences under § 924(j), invoking the principle that Congress does not lightly withdraw traditional judicial sentencing authority without express statement.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: As a strict textualist, the plain language of § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) controls: the consecutive sentencing mandate expressly applies to sentences imposed 'under this subsection,' and 'this subsection' unambiguously refers to § 924(c) itself, not § 924(j), which Congress explicitly designated as a separate and distinct subsection when enacted in 1994. The ordinary public meaning of 'this subsection' at the time of enactment would have been understood to refer to the specific subsection in which the language appears — § 924(c) — and not to a separate subsection that merely cross-references it; Congress knows how to write broadly applicable mandates when it intends to do so, and its choice to limit the language to 'this subsection' must be given effect. While the Government's structural argument that § 924(j) operates as an aggravated § 924(c) offense has surface appeal, it asks the Court to override clear statutory text based on inferred purpose — a methodology I have consistently rejected — and the rule of lenity further reinforces that any residual ambiguity must be resolved in the defendant's favor, as the statute imposes criminal punishment. The circuit consensus favoring the Government's position, while notable, does not override the textual analysis, and widespread judicial error does not transform incorrect statutory interpretation into correct law.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: As a textualist, I must examine the structural relationship between § 924(c) and § 924(j) carefully. Section 924(j) predicates criminal liability explicitly on a violation of § 924(c), making it functionally an aggravated form of the § 924(c) offense rather than a wholly independent provision — a defendant cannot be convicted under § 924(j) without first satisfying the elements of § 924(c). The consecutive sentencing mandate in § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) is therefore properly understood as traveling with the incorporated offense, because to hold otherwise would allow defendants who commit the most serious aggravated form of the offense — causing death — to paradoxically receive more lenient sentencing treatment than those convicted under the base § 924(c) provision. Furthermore, the overwhelming circuit consensus across six circuits supports this reading, and under United States v. Castleman, the rule of lenity applies only upon 'grievous ambiguity,' a threshold not met here given the structural dependency of § 924(j) on § 924(c) and the strong practical law enforcement interest in ensuring that the most culpable offenders face mandatory consecutive sentences.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The plain text of § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) expressly limits the consecutive sentencing mandate to terms imposed 'under this subsection,' and § 924(j) is a structurally distinct subsection that creates an independent offense — causing death through firearm use — rather than merely an aggravated sentencing enhancement under § 924(c). As then-Judge William Pryor persuasively reasoned in United States v. Julian, 633 F.3d 1250 (11th Cir. 2011), the statutory text cannot be stretched to carry the consecutive sentencing mandate across subsection boundaries without doing violence to the plain meaning of 'under this subsection.' From a pragmatic standpoint, allowing prosecutors to trigger mandatory consecutive sentencing simply by charging under § 924(j) rather than § 924(c) improperly transfers sentencing discretion from judges to prosecutors, undermining the individualized sentencing principles that protect defendants — particularly those from vulnerable communities who are disproportionately affected by mandatory minimums. Where genuine textual ambiguity exists, the rule of lenity further counsels in favor of the interpretation that preserves judicial discretion and avoids the harsher sentencing outcome.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The plain text of § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) limits the consecutive sentencing mandate to terms imposed 'under this subsection' — meaning § 924(c) itself — and a sentence imposed under § 924(j), a structurally distinct subsection, simply does not fall within that textual command. As a pragmatic textualist, I find the Eleventh Circuit's reasoning in United States v. Julian persuasive: § 924(j) uses § 924(c) only to shorthand its elements, but it is an independent offense with its own sentencing framework, including the possibility of life imprisonment or death — penalties that go well beyond § 924(c)'s graduated structure and signal congressional intent to create a separate provision. The rule of lenity, while not the primary driver here given Castleman's 'grievous ambiguity' threshold, reinforces this reading at the margins, and preserving judicial sentencing discretion under § 924(j) produces a more workable and coherent statutory scheme — one where judges, not prosecutorial charging decisions, calibrate the severity of consecutive versus concurrent sentences in the most serious cases. The Tenth Circuit's self-correction in Melgar-Cabrera, acknowledging it 'erred' in treating § 924(j) as a mere sentencing enhancement rather than a discrete crime, further confirms that the majority-circuit position rests on a structural misreading rather than a settled textual consensus.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The plain text of § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) expressly limits the consecutive sentencing mandate to terms 'imposed under this subsection' — meaning § 924(c) itself — and Congress's deliberate choice to codify § 924(j) as a separate, distinct subsection carries meaningful structural significance that courts must respect rather than paper over. Section 924(j) is not merely an aggravated penalty enhancement within § 924(c); it defines an independent offense — causing death through firearm use — with its own elements and punishment structure, much as this Court recognized in Castillo v. United States that structurally similar provisions created distinct crimes rather than sentencing factors. When Congress wanted the consecutive sentencing mandate to apply, it said 'under this subsection'; it did not say 'under this section' or 'under any provision incorporating this subsection,' and we are not at liberty to rewrite the statute to achieve what the Government wishes Congress had said. Even if one found the statutory relationship genuinely ambiguous after exhausting all textual and structural tools, the rule of lenity would require resolving that ambiguity in favor of the defendant, as the liberty interests at stake — potentially decades of additional imprisonment — demand that Congress speak clearly before courts impose such a severe mandatory consequence.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The text of § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) expressly limits the consecutive sentencing mandate to terms imposed 'under this subsection,' and § 924(j) is a distinct subsection that creates an independent offense with its own penalty structure — Congress's choice of 'subsection' rather than 'section' is a meaningful textual distinction that courts must respect. The superfluity argument is particularly compelling: if § 924(c)'s consecutive sentencing bar automatically traveled to § 924(j), then § 924(c)(5)(B)'s armor-piercing ammunition death provision would be rendered redundant, violating the canon against surplusage. While I am mindful of the strong circuit consensus favoring the Government's position — a factor I weigh seriously given my institutionalist concern for predictability and workability — that consensus does not override clear textual signals, and the Eleventh Circuit's reasoning in Julian reflects a more faithful reading of the statutory architecture. The rule of lenity under Castleman need not even be reached here because the text, structure, and superfluity canon together provide sufficient grounds to resolve the ambiguity in Lora's favor without resorting to that last-resort canon.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) expressly limits the consecutive sentencing mandate to terms imposed 'under this subsection,' and as an originalist and textualist, I must give those words their plain meaning — 'this subsection' refers to § 924(c), not § 924(j), which is a separate and distinct subsection. The structural canon that Congress's deliberate use of distinct subsection designations carries interpretive significance reinforces this reading; had Congress intended the consecutive sentencing mandate to apply to § 924(j), it could have said so explicitly, as it did with § 924(c)(5)(B). The Eleventh Circuit's reasoning in Julian is persuasive on the surplusage point: applying the concurrent-sentences bar to § 924(j) renders § 924(c)(5)(B) redundant, violating the canon against surplusage that this Court reaffirmed in TRW Inc. v. Andrews. While the weight of circuit authority runs against Lora, methodological consistency demands that I follow the text rather than a circuit consensus built on structural inference that overrides the statute's plain limiting language, and to the extent any ambiguity remains, the rule of lenity as a tiebreaker further supports the petitioner.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The plain text of § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii) expressly limits its consecutive sentencing mandate to terms imposed 'under this subsection,' and § 924(j) is a structurally distinct subsection that incorporates § 924(c)'s elements to define a separate, aggravated offense — not a sentence imposed under § 924(c) itself. As the Eleventh Circuit correctly recognized in United States v. Julian, the incorporation of § 924(c)'s elements into § 924(j) to establish liability does not sweep in § 924(c)'s sentencing provisions; expressio unius est exclusio alterius and the presumption against superfluity both counsel against reading § 924(j)'s limited cross-reference as a wholesale importation of § 924(c)'s sentencing mandates. The Sentencing Reform Act's default rule under 18 U.S.C. § 3584(a) — that concurrent sentencing governs absent a statutory mandate — combined with the rule of lenity applicable where Congress has not clearly spoken, preserves judicial sentencing discretion that is fundamental to individualized justice. My background as a public defender reinforces my concern that allowing prosecutorial charging decisions under § 924(j) versus § 924(c) to automatically trigger mandatory consecutive sentences effectively transfers sentencing discretion from judges to prosecutors, undermining the constitutional separation of powers in sentencing.

John Roberts.reasoning: The conference has reached a remarkable unanimity, and Justice Alito's conversion — driven precisely by the surplusage argument regarding § 924(c)(5)(B) that Justice Thomas and I identified as structurally decisive — confirms that the textual case for Petitioner is sound across methodological lines. Justice Alito's residual hesitation about the circuit consensus gives me pause as Chief Justice, since widespread circuit agreement sometimes signals that we are missing a genuine ambiguity, but here the circuits appear to have been misled by the structural dependency argument rather than by any genuine textual support for the Government's position. As I noted in my prior reasoning, the opinion should be written narrowly on the 'this subsection' plain meaning ground — § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii)'s consecutive mandate applies to sentences imposed under § 924(c), and § 924(j) is a separately lettered subsection defining a discrete offense — without reaching the rule of lenity, which would unnecessarily signal that the statute is ambiguous when the text is in fact clear. I will assign the majority opinion with instructions to ground the holding in the surplusage canon and the ordinary meaning of 'this subsection,' preserving the Court's institutional credibility by avoiding the appearance of result-oriented leniency while faithfully applying the text Congress enacted.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito raises the most serious counterargument — that § 924(j)'s structural dependency on § 924(c) as a predicate offense, combined with the anomalous result that the most aggravated offenders would receive more sentencing discretion than lesser offenders, suggests Congress intended § 924(j) to operate within § 924(c)'s sentencing framework. But this argument proves too much: structural dependency for purposes of establishing an element is categorically distinct from incorporation of sentencing rules, and as Justice Barrett correctly notes, Alleyne v. United States confirms that § 924(j) defines a discrete offense with its own elements — it is not merely a sentencing enhancement within § 924(c). The 'anomalous result' concern is a policy argument that cannot override the plain text; Congress routinely creates asymmetries in sentencing schemes, and it is not our role to correct perceived legislative oversights by stretching 'this subsection' beyond its ordinary meaning. The canon against surplusage further reinforces my position: if the consecutive mandate already applied to § 924(j), § 924(c)(5)(B)'s explicit treatment of the overlapping death-by-armor-piercing-ammunition scenario would be rendered superfluous, a result TRW Inc. v. Andrews instructs us to avoid.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: After careful reflection on my colleagues' arguments, I am persuaded to increase my confidence in the Petitioner's position. Justice Thomas's surplusage canon argument regarding § 924(c)(5)(B) remains the most compelling textual anchor — if the consecutive mandate already flowed through § 924(j)'s structural dependency on § 924(c), then Congress's explicit consecutive sentencing provision for the overlapping death-by-armor-piercing-ammunition scenario would be entirely superfluous, and TRW Inc. v. Andrews instructs us to avoid such readings. Justice Barrett's invocation of Alleyne v. United States also directly addresses my prior concern about structural dependency: the Court has already recognized that § 924(j) defines a discrete offense with its own jury-submissible elements, which means the sentencing authority for a § 924(j) conviction derives from § 924(j) itself rather than from § 924(c)'s framework. While the anomaly I identified — that death-causing defendants receive more sentencing discretion than those who merely brandish — remains troubling from a practical standpoint, Justice Gorsuch is correct that this is ultimately a policy concern for Congress to address, not a textual basis for stretching 'this subsection' beyond its ordinary meaning, particularly given § 3584's default rule preserving judicial discretion absent clear congressional override.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito raises the most serious challenge to our position — the structural dependency argument and the apparent anomaly that defendants convicted of the most aggravated conduct under § 924(c) would receive more sentencing flexibility than those who merely brandish a weapon. But this argument conflates structural dependency with sentencing incorporation. As Justice Barrett correctly notes, Alleyne v. United States confirms that § 924(j) defines a discrete offense with its own elements, not merely a sentencing enhancement within § 924(c); the sentencing authority for a § 924(j) conviction derives from § 924(j) itself, not from § 924(c). The 'anomaly' Justice Alito identifies actually reflects Congress's deliberate choice to treat the most serious conduct — causing death — as a separate, more serious offense subject to its own sentencing regime, including the possibility of death or life imprisonment, which itself represents a far more severe potential punishment than any § 924(c) mandatory minimum. Moreover, the surplusage problem Justice Thomas and Justice Roberts identify — that the Government's reading renders § 924(c)(5)(B) entirely redundant — is a powerful structural signal that Congress did not intend to import § 924(c)'s consecutive mandate into § 924(j), and the default rule under § 3584 preserves judicial discretion absent clear congressional override.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The conference has reached a remarkable degree of convergence, and I find Justice Alito's ultimate capitulation — driven precisely by the surplusage argument Justice Thomas and Justice Roberts identified regarding § 924(c)(5)(B) — to be the most telling development of this round. The structural dependency argument that initially gave me pause, and that Justice Alito pressed most forcefully, ultimately fails because it conflates two analytically distinct questions: whether § 924(j) requires § 924(c) conduct as an element, and whether § 924(j) sentences are imposed 'under' § 924(c)'s sentencing framework. Justice Barrett's invocation of Alleyne v. United States remains decisive on this point — once we recognize that § 924(j) defines a discrete offense with its own jury-submissible elements, the Government's structural incorporation theory loses its foundation. I write separately to note that while the rule of lenity provides an additional backstop, as Justice Roberts suggests, the majority opinion should rest primarily on the plain textual meaning of 'this subsection' and the surplusage canon, which together provide the most institutionally durable and least controversial basis for the holding.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito raises the most serious counterargument — that § 924(j)'s structural dependency on § 924(c) as a predicate element suggests it operates within § 924(c)'s broader sentencing framework, and that the anomaly of giving more discretion to defendants who cause death than those who merely brandish weapons is difficult to explain. But this argument proves too much: structural dependency for elements does not automatically import sentencing rules, and Congress routinely creates aggravated offenses that carry different — sometimes more flexible — sentencing regimes than their predicate offenses. Justice Barrett's point about Alleyne v. United States is particularly decisive here: the Court has already recognized that § 924(j) defines a discrete offense with its own elements that must be submitted to a jury, which fatally undermines the Government's claim that § 924(j) is merely a sentencing enhancement 'under' § 924(c). The anomaly Justice Alito identifies is real, but it is a policy concern that Congress — not this Court — must address; our role is to apply the text as written, and 'under this subsection' means § 924(c), not § 924(j). The default rule in § 3584 and the rule of lenity provide additional textual and constitutional backstops that reinforce what the plain text already compels.
